title: One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems - Nature Energy
gist: Fourier analysis of grid frequency in 12 grids on five continents reveals a persistent, phase-coherent 1-minute oscillation traced to clock-synchronized self-tests in battery-based UPS and battery energy storage control software, propagating from building level to the 110-kV grid. The amplitude is growing with data centres, batteries, IoT and falling inertia, and is already causing hydropower wear and regulatory change.

insights.claim: Grid frequency time series from 12 grids on five continents, from Iceland (about 400,000 customers) to Continental Europe (over 400 million), all show a narrow spectral peak at exactly 1 minute.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A universal deterministic disturbance means grid balancing cannot treat minute-scale frequency noise as purely random.
insights.locator: A universal 1-min pattern in the grid frequency

insights.claim: The 1-minute waveform stays phase-coherent over multiple years across all grids, which is hard to reconcile with intrinsic system oscillation modes and points to drivers synchronized to a stable external clock.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Shifts diagnosis from physics-based resonance to software timing, a new class of grid risk.

insights.claim: In the Continental European grid the pattern is stronger by day than at night and in summer than winter, with the frequency highest at the start of each minute then falling for seconds to half a minute, implying demand exceeds generation in the first half of each minute.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Daytime and summer strength matches load of digital equipment, supporting a demand-side cause.

insights.claim: In the Continental European grid, a 3 mHz periodic frequency variation corresponds to roughly 80 MW of coherent power variation, using a network power-frequency characteristic of 26.68 GW per Hz.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Gives scale: tens of MW of synchronized load swings are enough to move system frequency measurably.
insights.locator: Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

themes.theme: UPS and battery software as the source

insights.claim: Battery-based uninterruptible power supplies, specifically their battery energy management system self-tests, are identified as prime drivers: all four Jülich campus buildings with a clear 1-minute power signal contain battery UPSs, while none of the buildings without UPS show it.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Backup-power and battery control firmware becomes a grid-relevant asset class for operators and regulators.
insights.locator: Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

insights.claim: Narrow current peaks every minute at a UPS battery's DC terminals were confirmed by the manufacturer to be periodic self-tests, and the resulting power demand pattern was traced across transformers and a bus bar up to the 110-kV public grid connection.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Shows a small device-level routine propagates to transmission level; aggregation across fleets matters.
insights.locator: Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

insights.claim: With NTP time synchronization enabled, the UPS self-test timing shifts by about 6 seconds per day in steps at midnight UTC, indicating internally scheduled 1-minute cycles that are periodically re-initialized by external clock synchronization.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Clock sync is the coupling mechanism that aligns many independent devices, so time-sync infrastructure is a systemic dependency.
insights.locator: Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

insights.claim: UPS units from different manufacturers behave differently: one shows a drifting sawtooth waveform while two others show phase-stable demand peaks shortly after each minute begins, so energy management system implementation determines the grid impact.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Vendor firmware choices, not hardware class, decide whether a fleet is destabilizing.
insights.locator: Identifying the drivers of the 1-min pattern

insights.claim: The synchronization mechanism is not specific to UPSs or batteries but reflects a general property of digitally controlled devices using external timing signals or periodic software routines; a smart baking oven and Raspberry-Pi clusters also showed periodic power signatures at 1-minute and 30-second periods.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Broad class of risk extending to household IoT and any clocked control software.

themes.theme: Growth drivers: data centres, batteries, inertia

insights.claim: In Ireland, where data centres reached about 18% of national electricity demand in 2022 (Germany about 3%), the 1-minute frequency drop grew from roughly 3 mHz to 12 mHz between 2016 and 2021, with individual drops now exceeding 20 mHz.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Data-centre-heavy grids are the leading indicator; Irish-style grid constraints may become a siting factor for data-centre expansion.

insights.claim: Declining system inertia amplifies the frequency response to a given coherent power imbalance; in Mallorca, withdrawal of a major coal plant at the end of 2019 coincided with about a 50% increase in the 1-minute amplitude, although frequency-control changes may also have contributed.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Renewables-driven inertia loss makes small synchronized loads more consequential, supporting demand for synthetic inertia and fast frequency response.

insights.claim: The signal can grow on both sides of the frequency response: coherent power variations rise as clocked devices (batteries, data-centre UPS, IoT) proliferate, while the same variations cause larger frequency deviations as inertia falls.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Two-sided amplification framework for assessing how fast the problem scales; the authors say this is not an imminent stability threat.

insights.claim: Battery energy storage capacities in Europe are projected to rise rapidly under ENTSO-E's Ten-Year Network Development Plan scenarios, increasing the number of digitally controlled devices that could synchronize.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Utility-scale BESS rollout raises both the opportunity and the need for control-software standards.

insights.claim: In the Scandinavian grid the 1-minute amplitude regularly exceeded 10 mHz, contributing to wear and tear of hydropower turbines providing primary control, and the amplitude rose in the British and Scandinavian grids after 2015, peaking in 2020 around COVID-19 lockdowns.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Hydropower operators bear maintenance cost from digital-induced oscillation; a hidden cost of the energy transition.

insights.claim: Scandinavian transmission operators revised frequency containment reserve (FCR-N) requirements in 2023, adding sine-wave prequalification tests from 10 to 300 s and stricter damping, after which amplitudes above 10 mHz were no longer observed in 2025; Australia's 2020 primary frequency response mandate also reduced the signal.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Frequency-reserve rules are tightening; providers of fast, well-damped response may benefit, while poorly damped hydropower and batteries face compliance cost.

insights.claim: System-level regulation mitigates only the frequency response to the oscillation, not the underlying coherent power modulation, so it does not fix the root cause.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Regulatory fixes are partial; expect further control-design standards for batteries and UPS.

insights.claim: The root cause can be addressed through control design: clocked routines should avoid simultaneous power adjustments across many devices using randomized scheduling, adaptive offsets or event-driven rather than strictly time-driven execution.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Cheap software fix at the source; vendors that ship desynchronized scheduling reduce grid-code risk.

insights.claim: After the authors contacted the UPS manufacturer, a software update removed strict periodicity of current peaks in one battery block, though self-tests still occur at discrete times so the root cause is only partially resolved.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Shows over-the-air firmware can fix fleet-wide behaviour for utility-scale assets.

insights.claim: Mitigation is harder for household-scale IoT devices than for utility-scale batteries and UPS systems, because software updates and control standards are less coordinated for household devices.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Residential device fleets are the unmanaged tail risk; standards bodies and regulators will need to engage.

insights.claim: The authors argue power-system stability analysis must treat control logic, software timing and synchronization as integral components, and that even partial temporal coherence across large device populations may produce measurable aggregate effects.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Grid planning and cyber-risk assessment should widen to include benign software synchronization, not only attacks and failures.
